title: Declaring and Initialising Variables
theory: A declaration introduces a variable's type and name. Assignment stores a value. Initialisation gives a variable its first value, often in the declaration.
Combining declaration and initialisation is clear because the starting state is immediately visible. Separate them when the value is only known after another operation.
Fields receive automatic defaults, but local variables must be definitely assigned before they can be read.
The default keyword requests a type's default value: int becomes 0 and bool becomes false.
Use descriptive camelCase names. Avoid unexplained abbreviations and do not include the type in the name.
terms: The first value assigned to a variable.
A variable declared inside a method or block.
A variable declared as part of a type.
A naming style such as favouriteColour.
tryIt: Declare one variable separately, then create three variables using combined declaration and initialisation.
challenge: Write eight clearly named variables: four with separate assignment and four with combined initialisation.
mistakes: Assign local variables before reading them.
Do not use spaces or leading digits in names.
summary: Declaration introduces type and name, assignment stores a value, and initialisation supplies the first value.
quiz: int total; introduces the type and name only.
The declaration includes the first value.
Can an unassigned local int be printed?
Local variables must be definitely assigned.
The default Boolean value is false.
